SMTO-GWT-0073 — The GPU is busy with other work right now

GUID: 7bcc9e03-1915-5328-96c6-5dd4c9b08528
Slug: gpu-resource-busy
Domain: GWT · Subsystem: gpu

What happened

  • SMTO didn't make this GPU change because something else is using the card: a Local AI model is starting or running, another GPU change is in progress, or too many GPU requests are active. Nothing was changed.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. If you use Local AI on that computer, ask SMTO to list its Local AI runtimes, and stop any you no longer need. SMTO won't change GPU settings while a Local AI model it manages is starting or running on that card.
  2. Wait for any other task that is changing this GPU's settings to finish before asking again. Only one change at a time is allowed on each GPU, and the Gateway accepts at most 16 GPU requests at once.
  3. Once the other work is done, ask SMTO for the GPU change again. The request was turned away before anything ran, so repeating it is safe once the card is free.

What success looks like

  • SMTO accepts the GPU change and reports its result.

If it still fails

  • If it is still busy after the other work has finished, select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO; the details name the job holding the GPU, which may need them to check it. Don't force-quit programs on the GPU to free it.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • GPU admission was refused because the Local AI runtime lock was held or a live Local AI runtime owns the GPU, 16 GPU operations were already active, or a Gateway job holding this GPU UUID blocked admission.

What this means

  • GPU admission encountered a held runtime lock, a live owned model, a GPU ownership conflict, the sixteen-active-operation limit or a job that was not admitted. The retained phase, target and receipt determine what executed. Rendering this definition adds no probe, retries, dispatch or changes to resource ownership.

Why this can happen

  • GPU admission encountered a held runtime lock, a live owned model, a GPU ownership conflict, the sixteen-active-operation limit or a job that was not admitted.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect retained blocking jobs, local AI ownership and active operation count; distinguish a transient lock from a running workload.

How to fix it

  • Check the error details for gateway_job_id and blocking_job_ids and inspect those Gateway jobs; let Local AI runtimes on that node finish or stop them (resource locking for gpu.operation enforces this). A blocking GPU job in an unknown state keeps its claim until its effect is reconciled, so resolve it rather than waiting. Retry once the owners release the GPU; do not kill GPU clients or override existing claims.
  • Inspect the reported owner or capacity limit. Let existing work settle or stop it through its owning controls before requesting the GPU action.

Retry and execution caution

  • Inspect existing jobs and runtime ownership, then request the operation when those resources are free.

How to verify the fix

  • Existing owners settle and the requested GPU operation is admitted without replacing their claims.

What not to do

  • Do not replay uncertain mutations, kill GPU clients automatically or invent sensor values.

Technical notes

  • The retained phase, target and receipt determine what executed. Rendering this definition adds no probe, retries, dispatch or changes to resource ownership.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
